senses.definition: (transitive, archaic) To instruct, train (usually in matters of knowledge).

quotes.text: For he would learn their business secretly, / And then inform his master hastily.
quotes.reference: 1591, Ed[mund] Sp[enser], “Prosopopoia. Or Mother Hubberds Tale.”, in Complaints. Containing Sundrie Small Poemes of the Worlds Vanitie. […], London: […] William Ponsonbie, […], →OCLC:

quotes.text: I am informed thoroughly of the cause.
quotes.reference: c. 1596–1598 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Merchant of Venice”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London: […] Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene i]:

senses.definition: To act as an informer; denounce.
(transitive) To give form or character to; to inspire (with a given quality); to affect, influence (with a pervading principle, idea etc.).
examples: His sense of religion informs everything he writes.

quotes.text: But others declare that no Creature can be made or tranſmuted into a better or vvorſe, or transformed into another ſpecies or ſimilitude, by man, or devill. […] Martinus [i.e., Martin] Delrio the Jeſuit accounts this degeneration of Man into a Beaſt to be an illuſion, deceptive and repugnant to Nature; for, the ſoule of man cannot informe a beaſts body, […]
quotes.reference: 1653, John Bulwer, “Scene XXIIII. Cruell and Fantasticall Inventions of Men Practised upon Their Bodies in a Supposed Way of Bravery, and Wicked Practices both of Men and Devils to Alter and Deforme the Humane Fabricke”, in Anthropometamorphosis: Man Transform’d; or, The Artificial Changling […], 2nd edition, London: […] William Hunt, →OCLC, page 521:

quotes.text: Let others better mould the running mass / Of metals, and inform the breathing brass
quotes.reference: 1697, Virgil, “The Sixth Book of the Æneis”, in John Dryden, transl., The Works of Virgil: Containing His Pastorals, Georgics, and Æneis. […], London: […] Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC, page 397, lines 1169-1170:

quotes.text: O! long as breath informs this fleeting frame / Ne'er let me pass in silence Dorset's name
quotes.reference: 1858, Matthew Prior, The poetical works of Matthew Prior, Edinburgh: Printed by Ballantyne and Company, page 120, line 401:

quotes.text: WikiLeaks did not cause these uprisings but it certainly informed them. The dispatches revealed details of corruption and kleptocracy that many Tunisians suspected, but could not prove, and would cite as they took to the streets.
quotes.reference: 2013 June 7, Gary Younge, “Hypocrisy lies at heart of Manning prosecution”, in The Guardian Weekly, volume 188, number 26, page 18:

senses.definition: (intransitive, obsolete) To make known, wisely and/or knowledgeably.

examples: Don’t forget the code of ethics that informs this profession.

senses.definition: (intransitive, archaic) To take form; to become visible or manifest; to appear.

quotes.text: It is the bloody business which informs / Thus to mine eyes.
quotes.reference: c. 1606 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Macbeth”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London: […] Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene i]:

senses.definition: Without regular form; shapeless; ugly; deformed.

quotes.text:
Bleak Crags, and naked Hills,
And the whole Prospect so inform and rude
quotes.reference: 1765, Charles Cotton, “Wonders of Peake”, in Poetical Works, page 342:
